title: Bispecific T-Cell Engager Glofitamab in Relapsed or Refractory Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Multicenter Phase 2 Study
authors: Hutchings M, Carlo-Stella C, Bachy E, Offner F, Park D, Sureda A, Trneny M
abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Patients with relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) who experience treatment failure after chemoimmunotherapy have a poor prognosis. METHODS: In this pivotal multicenter phase 2 trial, 155 patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who had received at least two prior lines of systemic therapy were treated with fixed-duration glofitamab monotherapy administered intravenously for up to 12 cycles following obinutuzumab pretreatment. The primary endpoint was complete response rate assessed by an independent review committee. RESULTS: At a median follow-up of 12.6 months, complete response occurred in 61 of 155 patients (39.4%; 95% CI, 31.6 to 47.5), and an overall response occurred in 80 of 155 patients (51.6%; 95% CI, 43.5 to 59.7). The median duration of complete response was not reached, with 78% of complete responders remaining in response at 12 months. The most frequent adverse event was cytokine release syndrome (63.2%; grade 3 or 4, 3.9%). Discontinuations due to adverse events occurred in 9% of patients. CONCLUSIONS: Fixed-duration glofitamab induced frequent and durable complete remissions in heavily pretreated patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL, with manageable cytokine release syndrome.

title: Tirzepatide for Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis with Liver Fibrosis: A Double-Blind Phase 2 Randomized Trial
authors: Loomba R, Hartman ML, Lawitz EJ, Vuppalanchi R, Boursier J, Bugianesi E
abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a leading cause of cirrhosis and liver transplantation, with limited approved pharmacotherapies. METHODS: In this double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, 190 patients with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage F2 or F3 fibrosis were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide (5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg) or placebo for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was resolution of MASH without worsening of fibrosis on repeat liver biopsy at week 52. RESULTS: Resolution of MASH without worsening of fibrosis was achieved in 51.1% of patients receiving tirzepatide 5 mg, 55.6% receiving 10 mg, 62.2% receiving 15 mg, compared with 13.3% receiving placebo (P < 0.001 for all comparisons vs placebo). Improvement in fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening of MASH occurred in 54.5% of the pooled tirzepatide cohort versus 29.8% in the placebo group (P = 0.005). Common adverse events included nausea, diarrhea, and constipation, primarily mild-to-moderate and transient. CONCLUSIONS: Tirzepatide treatment for 52 weeks resulted in significant MASH resolution and clinically meaningful improvements in liver fibrosis compared to placebo.

title: Subcutaneous Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease: Pharmacokinetics, Safety, and Amyloid Clearance
authors: Irizarry M, van Dyck CH, Swanson CJ, Dhadda S, Bateman RJ, Honig LS
abstract_text: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the pharmacokinetics, safety, and amyloid plaque reduction of weekly subcutaneous lecanemab compared with biweekly intravenous dosing in early Alzheimer's disease. METHODS: In an open-label substudy of the Clarity AD trial, 72 patients received weekly subcutaneous lecanemab (720 mg) auto-injections, and were evaluated against the historical intravenous cohort (10 mg/kg biweekly). Primary measures included 14-week area under the curve (AUC), amyloid PET centiloid reduction, and incidence of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema (ARIA-E). RESULTS: Subcutaneous dosing demonstrated 11% higher steady-state AUC compared to intravenous administration. Brain amyloid plaque reduction at 6 months was comparable between subcutaneous (-59.2 centiloids) and intravenous (-54.6 centiloids) arms. ARIA-E occurred in 13.9% of the subcutaneous group compared to 12.6% in the intravenous group. Systemic injection-related reactions were substantially lower with subcutaneous administration (1.4% vs 26.4%). CONCLUSIONS: Weekly subcutaneous lecanemab achieved robust amyloid clearance and pharmacokinetic exposure equivalent to biweekly intravenous infusions, while dramatically reducing systemic infusion reactions.

title: Finerenone and Empagliflozin Dual Therapy in Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction
authors: Anker SD, Butler J, Filippatos G, Ferreira JP, Bocchi E, Bohm M
abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Both nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors independently improve outcomes in heart failure, but the safety and synergistic efficacy of their concurrent combination are unproven. METHODS: In a multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial, 840 patients with heart failure, NYHA class II-IV, and LVEF >40% were assigned to combination therapy (empagliflozin 10 mg plus finerenone 20 mg once daily) or empagliflozin monotherapy (10 mg daily) for 24 weeks. The primary outcome was change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score (KCCQ-TSS) at 24 weeks. RESULTS: At 24 weeks, the mean change in KCCQ-TSS was 8.6 points in the combination group versus 5.1 points in the monotherapy group (mean difference, 3.5 points; 95% CI, 1.8 to 5.2; P < 0.001). Significant reductions were observed in NT-proBNP levels (between-group ratio of geometric mean, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.72 to 0.91; P < 0.001). Hyperkalemia (potassium >5.5 mmol/L) occurred in 6.4% in the combination group versus 2.1% with monotherapy; no hyperkalemia-related deaths or emergency hospitalizations occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Combining finerenone with empagliflozin produced superior improvement in health status and symptom burden with an acceptable potassium safety profile in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction.

title: Aerosolized Bacteriophage Therapy as Adjunct to Antibiotics in Ventilator-Associated Multi-Drug Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pneumonia
authors: Pirnay JP, Djebara S, De Vos D, Verbeken G, Merabishvili M, Jennes S
abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa carries mortality rates exceeding 40% due to extreme antibiotic resistance. METHODS: In a double-blind, randomized phase 1/2 pilot trial, 48 mechanically ventilated ICU patients with confirmed multi-drug resistant P. aeruginosa pneumonia received standard intravenous targeted antibiotics plus either nebulized four-phage cocktail (10^9 PFU/mL twice daily for 7 days) or inhaled saline placebo. Primary outcomes were safety, 14-day bacterial clearance in bronchoalveolar lavage, and 28-day all-cause mortality. RESULTS: Bacteriophage aerosolization was well tolerated without therapy-associated bronchospasms or severe hypoxemia. Day 14 bacterial eradication occurred in 17 of 24 patients (70.8%) in the phage adjunct group compared with 9 of 24 patients (37.5%) receiving antibiotics alone (difference, 33.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.8 to 54.2; P = 0.038). All-cause 28-day mortality was 16.7% in the phage group versus 37.5% in the control group (HR 0.38; 95% CI, 0.15 to 0.98; P = 0.042). CONCLUSIONS: Inhaled phage cocktail administered alongside systemic antibiotics significantly increased pathogen clearance and reduced 28-day mortality in ventilator-associated resistant P. aeruginosa pneumonia.

title: Filgotinib versus Adalimumab in Inadequate Responders to Methotrexate for Active Rheumatoid Arthritis: 52-Week Results
authors: Combe B, Kivitz A, Tanaka Y, van der Heijde D, Matzkies F, Bartok B
abstract_text: OBJECTIVE: To compare the long-term clinical efficacy and radiographic progression between the selective JAK1 inhibitor filgotinib and TNF inhibitor adalimumab in active rheumatoid arthritis. METHODS: In this 52-week double-blind randomized controlled trial, 1755 active rheumatoid arthritis patients with inadequate response to methotrexate were randomized (3:3:2:3) to once-daily filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, subcutaneous adalimumab 40 mg biweekly, or placebo, all on stable background methotrexate. Primary endpoint was ACR20 response at week 12; key week 52 endpoints included DAS28-CRP <2.6 remission and radiographic progression (modified Sharp/van der Heijde score). RESULTS: At week 12, ACR20 was achieved by 76.6% on filgotinib 200 mg, 69.8% on filgotinib 100 mg, 71.1% on adalimumab, and 49.9% on placebo (P < 0.001 vs placebo). At week 52, DAS28-CRP <2.6 remission was achieved by 54.1% on filgotinib 200 mg versus 43.8% on adalimumab (treatment difference, 10.3%; 95% CI, 3.2% to 17.4%; P = 0.004). Inhibition of structural joint damage progression at week 52 was comparable between filgotinib 200 mg and adalimumab. Serious infection rates were 1.9% for filgotinib 200 mg and 1.8% for adalimumab. CONCLUSIONS: Filgotinib 200 mg once daily demonstrated statistically superior DAS28-CRP remission rates at 52 weeks compared to adalimumab, with sustained structural preservation and a consistent safety profile.
